Females attain a maximum adult body mass of 47 grams [Wwi = 47 grams], placing this species among the larger members of the genus Melozone. The oldest recorded individual, a female banded as a nestling in Monterey County, was recaptured at over 13 years of age, suggesting that the species' low annual reproductive investment is offset by remarkably high adult survival. This life-history strategy aligns with the predictions of slow-fast continuum models for temperate-zone passerines, where reduced fecundity is typically balanced by extended lifespan and stable population dynamics in relatively predictable Mediterranean-climate habitats.

Habitat selection in the California towhee is strongly tied to dense understory cover, particularly stands of coyote bush (Baccharis pilularis) and poison oak (Toxicodendron diversilobum). Foraging occurs primarily on the ground, where individuals use a characteristic double-scratch motion to uncover seeds and small invertebrates from beneath leaf litter. During the non-breeding season, flocks of up to fifteen individuals may form, though pairs remain territorial year-round in optimal habitat. The species exhibits limited sexual dimorphism, with males and females sharing similar plumage and behavioral roles during incubation and chick provisioning. Nest construction is entirely female-led, involving the assembly of coarse twigs and grasses into a cup-shaped structure, typically placed less than two meters above ground in dense shrubbery. Predation by western scrub-jays and domestic cats represents the primary source of nest failure, though the species' high adult survival buffers population declines.
